content: Many adolescents receive mentoring, but there has been no systematic review to determine whether mentoring effectively prevents alcohol and drug use. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of mentoring in preventing alcohol and drug use among adolescents. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including Cochrane CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, five other electronic databases, 11 grey literature databases, and 10 websites. Reference lists were reviewed, and experts in the fields of addiction and mentoring were consulted. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated mentoring interventions aimed at preventing alcohol and drug use in adolescents. From an initial pool of 2,113 abstracts, 233 full-text articles were independently assessed, and four RCTs met the inclusion criteria. These four studies included a total of 1,194 adolescents. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Investigators were contacted to obtain missing information. The four RCTs included in the review did not provide sufficient detail to determine whether robust randomization methods were used or whether allocation concealment was implemented. Blinding was not feasible due to the nature of the intervention, which involved mentoring. Three of the RCTs provided complete data, and there was no evidence of selective reporting. Regarding alcohol use, three RCTs provided evidence on the effectiveness of mentoring. Two of these studies were pooled, yielding a relative risk (RR) of 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57 to 0.90, P = 0.005) for mentoring compared to no intervention, indicating a statistically significant reduction in alcohol use. However, the third RCT found no significant differences between the mentoring and control groups. For drug use, three RCTs provided evidence, but their results could not be pooled due to differences in study design and outcomes. One study reported significantly lower use of illegal drugs in the mentoring group, while another found no significant differences. The third study focused solely on marijuana use and also found no significant differences. Additionally, one RCT measured substance use without distinguishing between alcohol and drugs and found no difference between the mentoring and control groups. All four RCTs were conducted in the United States and included adolescents from deprived backgrounds, with most participants belonging to minority groups. The participants were young, with two studies involving 12-year-olds and the other two including adolescents aged 9 to 16. At baseline, none of the participants were users of alcohol or drugs. Two RCTs demonstrated that mentoring reduced the rate of initiation of alcohol use, and one study showed a reduction in drug use initiation. However, the effectiveness of the interventions was limited by the low rates of alcohol and drug use initiation during the intervention period in two studies. For example, in one study, marijuana use increased to 1% in the experimental group and 1.6% in the control group, while in another study, drug use rose to 6% in the experimental group and 11% in the control group. In contrast, a third study showed a greater potential for the intervention to have an effect, as alcohol use increased to 19% in the experimental group and 27% in the control group. It is important to note that the studies assessed structured mentoring programs rather than informal mentoring relationships.
